newsitem.title: CHINA: Minister says China's prisons reform inmates.
newsitem.headline: Minister says China's prisons reform inmates.

text.p: China's Justice Minister Xiao Yang hailed the success of China's prison system on Friday, saying that only six to eight percent of convicts returned to a life of crime after their release.
"Lawful, strict, civilised and scientific management of prisons in China has produced good results," the China Daily quoted Xiao as saying.
The rate of reform among inmates in 1996 was above 90 percent with only between six and eight percent resuming criminal activities, among the lowest rates in the world, he said.
"This is a great advance," he said.
At the end of last year, China's prisons held 1.4 million inmates, accounting for 0.0113 percent of a total population of 1.2 billion, in China, he said.
This is among the lowest in the world, he said.
He did not include the numbers of those ordered to serve the administrative punishment of re-education through labour.

This penalty, imposed by the police rather than judicial authorities, has a maximum term of three years and is used by police to deal with petty offences and, more recently, to remove dissidents from public life.
Xiao dismissed overseas criticism of the conditions in China's prisons, saying its jails were intended to combine punishment with reform and to mix labour with education.

"China's prisons are not so evil and full of violence as described by some Western countries, but it is an active and self-reforming world," Xiao quoted an unidentified British inmate jailed in China as saying.
In 1996, the rate of escapes fell by 28 percent compared with the previous year while the rate of crime inside prisons declined by six percent from the previous year, Xiao said.
China has been promoting model prisons and re-education- through-labour centres since 1994 to improve conditions, Xiao said.
"Experience has proved that this has helped to reform prisoners and reduce crime," Xiao was quoted as saying.
